final.title: Table extraction works best as a workflow question
final.body:
If you are rethinking table extraction, do not start with the tool. Start with the workflow: which document are you handling, what table is inside it, and where does that data go after someone copies it out by hand? For a small business, that is usually invoice rows, order summaries, expense lines, or a lead spreadsheet.

The useful threshold is practical, not magical. AI table extraction fits best when the source is digital and consistent: exported PDFs, emails, or files with stable structure and little variation. It is a poor fit for scan-heavy, handwritten, or constantly changing documents. Bareni currently declines scan-heavy, OCR-dependent work, and its self-built demos do not implement PDF/scan ingestion or OCR, so that boundary matters.

The control pattern should stay human-led: AI extracts, a person validates, and the result lands in your own system. That is especially important where money movement or other high-risk decisions are involved; those still need human approval.

One practical next step is to ask yourself: how many hours a week does this re-entry take, and does it come from the same source each time? If the answer is yes, you have a bounded workflow worth diagnosing. If not, you probably need a better process before you need automation.

final.title: Table extraction works best as a workflow decision
final.body:
If you are rethinking table extraction, do not start with the tool. Start with the workflow: which document are you handling, what table lives in it, and where does the data go after a person would otherwise re-enter it by hand? For a small business, that is usually invoice rows, order summaries, expense lines, or a lead spreadsheet.

The useful threshold is simple. AI table extraction fits best when the source is digital and consistent: exports, PDFs, emails, or files with stable structure and little variation. It is a poor fit for scan-heavy, handwritten, or constantly changing documents. Bareni currently declines scan-heavy OCR-dependent work, so that boundary matters. That is current scope discipline, not a claim that the problem is impossible in principle.

The control pattern should stay human-led: AI extracts, a person validates, and the result lands in your own system. That matters even more when money movement or other high-risk decisions are involved, because those still need human approval.

One practical next step: ask yourself how many hours a week this re-entry takes, and whether it comes from the same source each time. If the answer is “same source, repeated work, clear table,” you have a bounded workflow worth diagnosing. If not, the process probably needs attention before automation does. The paper does not become less paper just because we asked nicely.
